lessons.title: ತಲೆ, ಕೈ — head and hand, the shared Dravidian core
lessons.gloss: head and hand — native Dravidian, matching Tamil/Malayalam closely

segments.text: Three languages, nearly one word each — Kannada's basic body parts line up with Tamil and Malayalam almost perfectly.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: The words

segments.text: ತಲೆ (tale) = "head" — native Dravidian, matching Tamil talai and Malayalam thala.
ಕೈ (kai) = "hand" — native Dravidian, matching Tamil and Malayalam's kai almost exactly.

segments.instruction: the match — nearly identical across Tamil, Malayalam, Kannada
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the match — nearly identical across Tamil, Malayalam, Kannada]

segments.text: What are Kannada's words for head and hand? (ತಲೆ tale, ಕೈ kai.) How closely do they match Tamil and Malayalam? (Very closely — all three share essentially the same native Dravidian words.)

lessons.title: ◌ಾ (ā) — one character, met inside words you already say
lessons.gloss: the single character ಾ — recognised inside words you already say

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ◌ಾ and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: ರ — what does it do?
One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
It is a vowel sign. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and replaces the a built into it with ā. Replaces, not adds — the a is gone.
You already say these, and every one of them has ◌ಾ (ā) somewhere inside it:
ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ namaskāra — hello / greetings (namaskāra — "a making of a bow").
ಧನ್ಯವಾದ dhanyavāda — thank you (dhanyavāda — "an utterance of 'worthy'").
ನೀವು ಹೇಗಿದ್ದೀರಾ? nīvu hēgiddīrā — how are you? (respectful).
ನಾನು nānu — I.
Put your pen on ◌ಾ (ā) and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.

segments.instruction: at these words, and find ◌ಾ (ā) in the ones that have it
segments.source: [YOU LOOK: at these words, and find ◌ಾ in the ones that have it]

segments.text: ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ, ಧನ್ಯವಾದ, ಹೌದು.

segments.instruction: ◌ಾ three times, saying ā as you finish each one
segments.source: [YOU TRACE: ◌ಾ three times, saying *ā* as you finish each one]

segments.instruction: back at any page of this chapter and find ◌ಾ (ā) once more
segments.source: [YOU LOOK: back at any page of this chapter and find ◌ಾ once more]

segments.text: Which character is this — ◌ಾ? What vowel does it put on the consonant it attaches to — and what does it take off? (Puts ā on; takes the built-in a off.) Name one word you already say that contains it.

lessons.gloss: the single character ಯ — recognised inside words you already say

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ಯ and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: ಕ — what does it do?
One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
ಯ — ya.
It is a consonant, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an a already in it. So it is not y, it is ya.
You already say these, and every one of them has ಯ (ya) somewhere inside it:
ಧನ್ಯವಾದ dhanyavāda — thank you (dhanyavāda — "an utterance of 'worthy'").
ದಯವಿಟ್ಟು dayaviṭṭu — please (dayaviṭṭu.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
